article.title: Thomas Frank on How the Promise of Progress Soured
article.author: Thomas Frank
article.content: The pundit and cultural historian Thomas Frank has again done what he does best: holding up an unflattering mirror to the extreme center. Where the object lesson of Frank’s 2016 book, Listen, Liberal , was the Democratic Party’s neoliberal, technocratic turn, and in his 2020 work, The People, No , he examined how populism turned from a lived political ideology into a self-serving cuss word, in his new book, The Creativity Con , Frank has unpicked the chattering classes’ infatuation with all things innovative. As the title gives away, that obsession has produced a con. The book traces the history of creativity thinking in the United States. Frank picks up the thread in the early twentieth century when some ad men (BBDO cofounder Alex Osborn is key here) promised US workers that creativity was a democratic virtue and that everyone could hone their abilities to come up with something new. Frank traces the story all the way to the likes of Richard Florida, who, as an academic and consultant, became rich and influential by selling town halls the world over policy recipes to remake their desolate, deserted neighborhoods into shiny launchpads for the creative class. Ideas, knowledge, and brainpower were supposed to become the commodities of the twenty-first century, while jobs “bending metal” had become the obsolete purview of the losers, the poor, and the uneducated. What was needed to attract the creatives, Florida explained, were lofts and bike paths and lattes, while the plight of the metal benders was treated as an afterthought. Frank takes us all the way to the present, with its return of geopolitical conflict and its shadow of technological disruption hanging over the life prospects even of the academically certified. He invites us readers to follow him along with his hilarious reportage (at South by Southwest), deep digs in libraries and archives (Alex Osborn again), and trips to cities where Florida and his ilk sold their magic. We also join Frank in parsing US presidential speeches filled to the brim with “innovation blather” (which he calls “innotalk”) and see him deconstruct weapons’ producers marketing material — in the process taking a swipe at Marianna Mazzucato’s modern classic The Entrepreneurial State for failing to note that all those big beautiful public innovations from Silicon Valley were meant to maim, kill, and destroy. These observations are interspersed with Frank’s more personal ruminations: on the world’s fairs his parents took him to; onthe fate of his artist friends in a world where Spotify has turned the music industry into a winner-takes-all market; and on the goals and aims of The Baffler , the countercultural magazine that he and friends set up in 1988. In its second part, the book pivots from a critical cultural history to a pamphlet of critical political economy. There Frank contrasts the shiny marketing rhetoric of the creatives and innovators with the material reality they have created. His verdict: the narrative of the United States as the harbinger of newness is, worse than bullshit, a camouflage to obscure that the best times lie not ahead of us but in the past. He concludes that what he calls “progressland” has actually produced a country in decline. For Jacobin , Ewald Engelen spoke with Frank about the function of “innotalk,” artificial intelligence, the midterms, the blue wave, cynicism, and the need to save the past from the future. Ewald Engelen The key to the book is the flip halfway through from scathing social criticism to the real world “innotalk” has produced. You describe its function as providing camouflage. Explain? Thomas Frank The word is used by different people to mean different things, but it’s always self-interested. It’s always performing some interest — it’s always some way of describing their interests as universal interests. But it does it by different methods. So, when Barack Obama uses the word “innovation,” it means something different than when defense contractors use it. But in both cases, they’re using it for really ugly purposes. Obama is using it to tell his base, Democratic voters, that he’s on board. He’s a progressive because it’s all about progress: innovation is progress. It’s change. And he’s also using it at the same time to tell Google: I hear you. I get it. So, it’s a word that’s extremely useful for him because he gets to have it both ways. But then with the defense contractors, it’s camouflage for their project, which is to loot the taxpayer. And the Pentagon — who really cares about national defense? These billion-dollar airplanes and destroyers that cost as much as nuclear aircraft carriers, these crazy things that always come with massive cost overruns and fail to perform: that’s not what this is about. It’s about pocketing the spoils of war. No more, no less. Ewald Engelen Your exercise in unmasking depends crucially on the 2016 book by the US economic historian Robert Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth . In it, he argues that productivity growth has stagnated since the late 1970s and that Big Tech, the smartphone, and the internet have failed to show up in productivity statistics. Is that still the case? What about the AI bubble and the potential wipeout of the creative class? Thomas Frank Wouldn’t that be something? After all these years, finally, finally. That would be appropriate, because I just finished working on this big project saying it hasn’t happened, and it would be hilarious if then it finally did happen right after I put the book out. So, I don’t know. Maybe tomorrow it’ll finally arrive. But look: productivity growth is nowhere near where it was in the 1940s or 1950s or 1960s. Maybe next year it will be, but we haven’t seen it so far. However, I have my doubts, for obvious reasons. There’s still a lot of brilliance in the world. There are still a lot of people coming up with new things. It’s just that the incentives are all arranged in such a way that the things they come up with do not add to the general wealth of the country. They add to the personal wealth of a small handful of people. We’ve arranged the incentives in a way that the general public and the economy as a whole don’t benefit much from all the stuff that people have dreamed up. Ewald Engelen The Creativity Con appeared a couple of weeks before the midterms. Did you see any signs on the side of Democrats that they have dropped “innotalk” and have shifted to a language of material needs? Thomas Frank Not in those terms, no. Nobody has. But indirectly, yes. There’s massive backlash against AI and the data centers. And also, Donald Trump’s basically aligning himself with the billionaire elite, specifically Elon Musk. Right now, Jensen Huang was in the news because he was basically [Trump’s] second-best friend after Elon. All of that really came back to bite him, thank goodness. The other thing that’s interesting is Barack Obama, who is still regarded and probably will be forever regarded by most Democrats as something of a saint. So, I went to the opening day at the Obama library. In it, he has reimagined his own history so that he is the descendant and legatee of all the great reform movements of the past. He is the culmination of the civil rights movement. He’s the culmination of the women’s suffrage movement. He’s the culmination of progressivism. He’s the culmination of the antiwar movement of the 1960s. All these things. There’s this elaborate museum, and the first story of the museum is all about these various left-wing social movements of the past. And they all lead to this one guy, Barack Obama. The exhibit on innovation is on the top story. He doesn’t leave it out, but it’s not emphasized as much as it was during his presidency — implying that his faith in innovation has now gone out of fashion. Ewald Engelen What about the Financial Times claiming that the Democrats won because they replaced identity-talk with class-talk? Thomas Frank Well, yes. In that sense, it’s a good thing. In that sense, yes, I’m very hopeful about it. But these are the Democrats we’re talking about. They will disappoint you every time. Look, I’m sixty-one years old. I’ve been a very cynical person. And cynicism has served me pretty well. So, I’m not going to all of a sudden say, “We’ve turned a corner and this is great.” By the way, the centrist faction in the Democratic Party is fighting back pretty hard right now. And they’re claiming that the election was not about those things. It was actually about their things. This is what they do in America. They have an election, and then they fight about what it actually meant. Ewald Engelen In the book, you call yourself a scoffer by trade. Why? Thomas Frank That’s pure H. L. Mencken, the Baltimore newspaper man. He had this very witty, scathing, vicious style. A man of incredible perceptiveness, but who had really lousy politics, really kind of ugly libertarian politics. He hated everything and everybody, he but had this astonishing power to penetrate the surface of things. I read him starting in high school and was always convinced that that was missing from the way the Left talked, the way the Left wrote about politics back in the day when I started. It’s also an automatic stance of skepticism toward whatever you see on serious television or read in serious newspapers and whatever you hear on serious radio. There is no intellectual fun in debunking Fox News. There is in reading a New York Times op-ed from a mainstream political scientist professor against the grain. Ewald Engelen The final sentence of the book reads: “Spotify pulls up the Clash for me, a creative work I remember not just liking, but believing in when I was 19. Yet somehow it sounds all wrong now, impossible to understand, some frantic noise from another age, another civilization, a world that is no more.” That is pure nostalgia, isn’t it? Thomas Frank What I am commenting upon here is directly taken from the British historian E. P. Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class , where at the end he talks about saving the past from the “enormous condescension of posterity.” His book, as well as mine, is a clarion call against forgetfulness, against obsolescence — the obsolescence of humans as well as machines. And I was really feeling it. I was on vacation with my daughter. We were in Japan, and I was in an enormous train station in Tokyo. Enormous. And then Spotify, the machine, pulled up a song I was listening to when I was nineteen, bringing forcefully home the downside of progress: obsolescence, and also alienation and condescension. Our condescension for the past, in this culture — in the culture of progress, the culture where innovation is valued — our condescension for the past is enormous. In some sense, I’ve always been that guy. I want to be like E.P. Thompson. I want to rescue these people from the condescension of posterity. And the nous and acumen and political courage of the historical populists are the classic case. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
